Maintenance Report — MNT-0001-002

Asset: WELL-0001 (SW-23 Well 001, T200, Southwest Block 23) Equipment: flowline Work started: 17 Mar 2023 08:00 · Finished: 18 Mar 2023 04:00 · Well stopped for this job: 20 hours Crew lead: Kevin Price (U-303) · Crew: Daniel Foster, Megan Ward Triggered by: inspection INS-0001-0021 on 2023-03-16 Report written: 19 Mar 2023

What happened

The weekly manual inspection INS-0001-0021 at 14:00 on 2023-03-16 found crude oil on the pad: about 2.7% of the pad area, estimated 0.5 bbl. The inspector noted: "Dark staining on pad." The field operator shut the well in, closed the flowline valve and placed earth berms and absorbent pads. The release was contained about 5.3 hours after the inspection. The crew traced the leak to a threaded coupling on the flowline close to the wellhead.

Root cause

Thread fatigue from pump jack vibration.

Safety and permits

  • Pre-job safety meeting held with the crew before work started (WS-01).
  • Energy isolated: prime mover stopped at the bottom of the stroke, brake set and chained, motor disconnect locked and tagged, wellhead wing valve closed and tagged, pressure bled off (WS-02).
  • Personal H2S monitors worn; highest reading 0 ppm, below the 10 ppm stop-work level (WS-03).
  • Hot work permit issued for welding; gas test before welding read 3% LEL, below the 10% limit (WS-04).

Work done

  1. Excavated around the coupling.
  2. Cut out the failed coupling and the pipe ends.
  3. Welded in new pipe and a new fitting.
  4. Coated the new joints.
  5. Excavated the stained soil.
  6. Backfilled after the pressure test.

Summary of the fix: replaced leaking flowline section and remediated soil.

Testing and return to service

Pressure-tested the repaired section at 196 psi (1.25 × the flowline's maximum operating pressure of 157 psi) and held it for 4 hours with no pressure drop (WS-05). The well was returned to production.

Spill clean-up and waste

  • About 0.9 m³ of stained soil excavated, bagged and sent to an approved disposal site under waste manifest WM-0001-002 (WS-06).
  • 2 soil samples taken around the spill; the highest result after clean-up was 0.4% TPH, below the 1.0% target (SR-03).

Maintenance Report — MNT-0001-021

Asset: WELL-0001 (SW-23 Well 001, T200, Southwest Block 23) Equipment: pump jack Work started: 25 Jul 2025 08:00 · Finished: 26 Jul 2025 15:00 · Well stopped for this job: 31 hours Crew lead: Kevin Price (U-303) · Crew: Daniel Foster Triggered by: inspection INS-0001-0140 on 2025-07-24 Report written: 26 Jul 2025

What happened

On a very hot afternoon (air temperature 43.1 °C) the electric motor driving the pump jack tripped on thermal overload and the pump jack stopped. The drone thermal reading during inspection INS-0001-0140 showed the wellhead at 51.6 °C. That looks hot, but it was only 8.5 °C above the air temperature. For a T200 well that means the well was not producing: the warmth was from the sun, not from oil flowing.

Root cause

The motor's cooling fan shroud was cracked and was restricting airflow. In extreme heat the motor could not shed enough heat and the overload protection tripped, as designed.

Safety and permits

  • Pre-job safety meeting held with the crew before work started (WS-01).
  • Energy isolated: brake set and chained, motor disconnect locked and tagged (WS-02).
  • Personal H2S monitors worn; highest reading 0 ppm (WS-03).
  • No hot work needed.

Work done

  1. Checked the motor windings with an insulation tester: no damage found.
  2. Removed the cracked cooling fan shroud and fitted a new one.
  3. Cleaned dust from the cooling fins.
  4. Reset the motor overload.

Summary of the fix: reset motor overload, replaced cooling fan shroud.

Testing and return to service

Ran the unit for 2 hours: motor current within the nameplate rating and stroke rate normal. The well was returned to production.

Parts and cost

ItemUSD
Fan shroud450
Consumables190
Labour (about 11 crew-hours)900
Total1,540

Compliance check

Notes and recommendations

  • Check motor cooling on all pump jacks in this area before next summer.
  • Remind operators that a hot wellhead on a hot day does not mean the well is producing; compare with the air temperature.

Maintenance Report — MNT-0001-029

Asset: WELL-0001 (SW-23 Well 001, T200, Southwest Block 23) Equipment: flowline Work started: 12 Jun 2026 07:00 · Finished: 13 Jun 2026 18:00 · Well stopped for this job: 35 hours Crew lead: Daniel Foster (U-302) · Crew: Brian Coleman, Megan Ward · Contractor: Tumbleweed Flowline Co. Triggered by: inspection INS-0001-0185 on 2026-06-11 Report written: 15 Jun 2026

What happened

The weekly drone inspection INS-0001-0185 at 14:30 on 11 June 2026 found crude oil pooled around the flowline coupling about 6 m downstream of the wellhead. Roughly 9.4% of the pad was stained, an estimated 6.8 bbl. That is a reportable spill under the Spill Response SOP, and because it covered more than 5% of the pad the T200 manual requires an immediate shut-in. The field operator, Jake Morales, shut the well in that afternoon. The crew on call was finishing another job, so earth berms and absorbent pads were only in place in the evening: the release was contained about 7 hours after the inspection flight.

The spill report to the State Oil & Gas Commission was filed 41 hours after detection, on 13 June. The HSE on-call handover had been missed, so nobody owned the report on 11–12 June.

Root cause

The threaded coupling had external corrosion under a failed protective wrap. This is the second flowline failure in a month on this well: a pinhole leak was repaired on 10 May 2026 (MNT-0001-028). The flowline passed its annual integrity test on 7 March 2026 (MNT-0001-026). A pressure test does not reveal wall loss hidden under a wrap, so the weakness was missed.

Safety and permits

  • Pre-job safety meeting held with the crew and the contractor before work started (WS-01).
  • Energy isolated: prime mover stopped at the bottom of the stroke, brake set and chained, motor disconnect locked and tagged, wellhead wing valve and flowline valve closed and tagged, line pressure bled off (WS-02).
  • Personal H2S monitors worn; highest reading 2 ppm, below the 10 ppm stop-work level (WS-03).
  • Hot work permit issued for welding; gas test before welding read 0% LEL (WS-04).

Work done

  1. Removed free oil from the pad with a vacuum truck and absorbent pads.
  2. Excavated around the coupling and exposed 6 m of flowline.
  3. Cut out the failed coupling and 4 m of corroded pipe.
  4. Welded in new pipe and a new coupling, then wrapped the joint.
  5. Excavated the stained soil around the coupling and across the pad.

Summary of the fix: replaced coupling and 4 m of flowline; excavated and bagged contaminated soil.

Testing and return to service

Pressure-tested the repaired section at 196 psi (1.25 × the flowline's maximum operating pressure of 157 psi) and held for 4 hours with no pressure drop (WS-05). The well was returned to production at 18:00 on 13 June.

Spill clean-up and waste

  • About 3.3 m³ of stained soil excavated, bagged and shipped to an approved disposal site under waste manifest WM-0001-029 (WS-06).
  • 4 soil samples taken around the spill; the highest result after clean-up was 0.8% TPH, below the 1.0% target. Agency verification requested (SR-03).

Notes and recommendations

  • HSE to fix the on-call handover so reportable spills always have an owner.
  • Replace the whole flowline on this well instead of patching sections; two failures in a month show the line is in poor condition.
  • Add a visual check of coupling wraps to the flowline inspection, because pressure tests miss wall loss under a wrap.

Maintenance Report — MNT-0001-032

Asset: WELL-0001 (SW-23 Well 001, T200, Southwest Block 23) Equipment: flowline Work started: 02 Oct 2026 08:00 · Finished: 02 Oct 2026 19:00 · Well stopped for this job: 11 hours Crew lead: Kevin Price (U-303) · Crew: Megan Ward, Brian Coleman Triggered by: inspection INS-0001-0201 on 2026-10-01 Report written: 03 Oct 2026

What happened

The weekly drone inspection INS-0001-0201 at 09:45 on 2026-10-01 found crude oil on the pad: about 4.0% of the pad area, estimated 1.6 bbl. The inspector noted: "Dark staining on pad." The field operator shut the well in, closed the flowline valve and placed earth berms and absorbent pads. The release was contained about 1.7 hours after the inspection. The crew traced the leak to a threaded coupling on the flowline close to the wellhead.

Root cause

Thread fatigue from pump jack vibration. This is corrective repair number 3 on this well's flowline in the last 12 months.

Safety and permits

  • Pre-job safety meeting held with the crew before work started (WS-01).
  • Energy isolated: prime mover stopped at the bottom of the stroke, brake set and chained, motor disconnect locked and tagged, wellhead wing valve closed and tagged, pressure bled off (WS-02).
  • Personal H2S monitors worn; highest reading 1 ppm, below the 10 ppm stop-work level (WS-03).
  • Hot work permit issued for welding; gas test before welding read 2% LEL, below the 10% limit (WS-04).

Work done

  1. Excavated around the coupling.
  2. Cut out the failed coupling and the pipe ends.
  3. Welded in new pipe and a new fitting.
  4. Coated the new joints.
  5. Excavated the stained soil.
  6. Backfilled after the pressure test.

Summary of the fix: replaced leaking flowline section and remediated soil.

Testing and return to service

Pressure-tested the repaired section at 196 psi (1.25 × the flowline's maximum operating pressure of 157 psi) and held it for 4 hours with no pressure drop (WS-05). The well was returned to production.

Spill clean-up and waste

  • About 1.4 m³ of stained soil excavated, bagged and sent to an approved disposal site under waste manifest WM-0001-032 (WS-06).
  • 2 soil samples taken around the spill; the highest result after clean-up was 0.48% TPH, below the 1.0% target (SR-03).
